---
title: "biohttp"
subtitle: "A call returns a value. It never raises."
---

## The soup this replaces

```r
fetch_gene <- function(symbol) {
  url <- paste0("https://mygene.info/v3/query?q=", symbol)
  tryCatch(
    {
      body <- jsonlite::fromJSON(url)
      if (length(body$hits) == 0) return(NULL)
      body$hits[1, ]
    },
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
}
```

::: {.walls}
::: {.w1}
no such gene

NULL
:::

::: {.w2}
network down

NULL
:::

::: {.w3}
HTTP 503

NULL
:::

::: {.w4}
body was HTML

NULL
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
NULL erases why. A cache of NULLs poisons itself.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: The hand rolled client throws away the one thing the caller needs,
which is the reason.

SCRIPT: This is a lightly edited copy of a function from one of my apps.
Four different things produce that NULL: the gene does not exist, the
network is down, the service returned a 503, the body was an HTML
maintenance page. The UI says not found for all four. And the first time
somebody wraps this in a cache, the cache stores the NULL and keeps saying
not found after the outage ends.

NUMBERS: 4 causes, 1 NULL.

HONESTY: Not a strawman. I wrote it.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 0:50.

IF ASKED: "Isn't httr2 enough?" httr2 is the engine here. biohttp is the
policy on top: what gets cached, what trips the breaker, what a failure looks
like to the caller.
:::

## ![](../assets/logos/biohttp.svg){.titlelogo} The one rule

::: {.kicker}
A call returns a value. It never raises.
:::

![](../assets/diagrams/envelope-flow.svg){.nostretch width="90%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
ONE JOB: Four different outcomes on the wire, one shape back, every time.

SCRIPT: Whatever happens on the wire, the caller gets the same envelope. A
transport failure, a non-2xx, a 2xx whose body will not parse, and a real
answer all come back as a list with the same fields. There is no tryCatch
at the call site because there is nothing to catch. You branch on status.

NUMBERS: 4 outcomes, 1 envelope, 9 fields.

HONESTY: biohttp knows nothing about biology. It never will.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 1:40.

IF ASKED: "What about a parse error in my own code?" That is your bug, and
it should raise. The rule is about the transport, not your parser.
:::

## Nine fields

| field | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `ok` | TRUE only when status is `ok`. Derived. |
| `status` | one of seven. What you branch on. |
| `http` | the code, or NA when nothing arrived |
| `data` | the parsed body on success |
| `error` | one sentence for the user |
| `detail` | the technical cause, for the log |
| `retry_after` | seconds the service asked you to wait |
| `source`, `ts` | who answered, when |

::: {.payoff}
`error` goes on screen. `detail` goes in the log. Never the other way round.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: The user-facing sentence and the technical cause are separate
fields, so neither ever leaks into the wrong place.

SCRIPT: Nine fields. ok is derived from status so the two cannot disagree.
The split I care most about is error versus detail. Error is a sentence fit
for a user: MyGene is temporarily unavailable. Detail is the cause: MyGene
returned HTTP 503. Render one, log the other, and a stack trace never reaches
a bench scientist while your log never loses one.

NUMBERS: 9 fields.

HONESTY: retry_after is new in 0.1.3. On CRAN 0.1.2 the envelope has eight.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 2:30.

IF ASKED: "Why source in the envelope?" So the error sentence names the
service without the caller formatting it.
:::

## Seven statuses

::: {.pills .big}
[ok]{.ok} [no_data]{.alt} [stale]{.alt} [rate_limited]{.warm} [timeout]{.warm} [skipped]{.mute} [error]{.warm}
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.teal}
`no_data`

An answer, not a fault. The source was reached and has nothing.
:::

::: {}
`skipped`

Nothing was sent. The host is paused. Evidence about the host, not the query.
:::

::: {.teal}
`stale`

Real data, past its freshness window. `ok` is FALSE so it never gets cached.
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Three of the seven are the ones a hand rolled client collapses into "failed".
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: no_data and skipped are answers about different things, and
telling them apart is why the enum exists.

SCRIPT: Seven levels, best to worst. The three people miss: no_data means
the service said there is nothing here, which is information. Skipped means
we did not ask, because the host is paused, which says nothing about your
query. Stale means we have data but it is old. A hand rolled client folds
all three into failed, and the UI shows the wrong message.

NUMBERS: 7 statuses.

HONESTY: stale is a constructor for client code to use; the transport
itself never emits it.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 3:20.

IF ASKED: "Is a 404 always no_data?" For a lookup API, yes. For a
misconfigured URL it would also be no_data, which is a bug you will see in
detail.
:::

## Branching

```r
switch(res$status,
  ok           = render_table(res$data),
  no_data      = "Nothing found for that query.",
  skipped      = "Source paused, try again shortly.",
  rate_limited = paste("Slow down, retry in", res$retry_after, "s"),
  res$error
)
```

::: {.flow}
::: {}
handle what you can act on

ok, no_data, skipped, rate_limited
:::

::: {}
let the rest fall through

`res$error` is already a sentence
:::

::: {}
`body_or_null()`

When you honestly do not care why
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Every branch is testable offline with one mocked response.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: Branching on status is one switch, and the default branch is
already a sentence.

SCRIPT: This is the whole call site. A switch on status. Handle the cases
you have a UI for, and let the rest fall through to res dollar error, which
is already fit to show. body_or_null collapses the envelope to the body or
NULL for the cases where the failure is genuinely not actionable. Reach for
it to save typing, not to avoid reading the envelope.

NUMBERS: 1 switch.

HONESTY: None.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 4:00.

IF ASKED: "How do I test the branches?" httr2 with_mocked_responses, one
status code per test. The tutorial produces all seven in one chunk.
:::

## The breaker rule

::: {.verbatim}
"Only a transport failure counts against a host. Any HTTP response at all,
including a 500 and including a 200 whose body will not parse, proves the
host is reachable and clears the count."

[from the biohttp vignette]{.src}
:::

::: {.bignums}
::: {}
3

failures to open
:::

::: {}
120

seconds cooldown
:::

::: {.zero}
0

requests while open
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
A 503 proves the host is up. Taking it out of rotation turns a partial outage into a total one.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: A 500 must not trip the breaker, and this is the rule hand rolled
breakers most often get wrong.

SCRIPT: After three consecutive transport failures a host is skipped for
two minutes. The rule that matters is what counts as a failure. Only a
transport failure: DNS, refused, timed out. Any HTTP response, a 500, a 200
carrying garbage, proves the host is reachable and clears the count. A
service returning error pages is broken, but it is up, and taking it out of
rotation turns a partial outage into a total one.

NUMBERS: 3 failures, 120 s, both configurable by env var.

HONESTY: It heals by itself. breaker_reset exists for tests and demos.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 4:50.

IF ASKED: "Per host or per URL?" Per host. One dead endpoint on a live
host does not pause the host.
:::

## Success-only cache

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Stored**

- a 2xx that parsed

**Never stored**

- timeout, refused, 5xx
- `no_data` from a 404
- `stale`, `skipped`

Failures are fetched again every time.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
| variable | default |
|---|---|
| `BIOHTTP_CACHE_TTL` | 1800 s |
| `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DISK` | off |
| `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DIR` | `R_user_dir()` |
| `BIOHTTP_CACHE_DISK_TTL` | 7 days |
| `BIOHTTP_CACHE_SALT` | empty |

Per call: `ttl = 86400` for a bulk table.
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Disk tier on, salt fixed, TTL long: a committed cache replays a whole demo offline.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: Only successes are cached, and with the disk tier and a fixed
salt, the cache is a reproducibility tool.

SCRIPT: A cache that stores a failure poisons itself for the life of the
process. So biohttp never does. Memory by default, disk opt in through
environment variables, because a library should not start writing to your
disk because you installed it. This repo turns the disk tier on, points it
inside the project, fixes the salt, sets the lifetime to a year, and commits
the directory. Every tutorial and the app replay from it with the network
off.

NUMBERS: 7 variables; 30 min default TTL; 7 day disk ceiling.

HONESTY: A year long TTL is a demo device. In production use the defaults.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 5:40.

IF ASKED: "What is the salt for?" It is in the cache key. A shared disk
cache without one collides across app versions and leaks which queries ran.
:::

## Many questions, one host

```r
transport_stats_reset()
res <- get_json_many(
  "https://mygene.info/v3", path = "query",
  queries = lapply(c("BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR"), \(g) list(q = g)),
  source = "MyGene",
  throttle = list(capacity = 10, fill_time_s = 60)
)
transport_stats()
#>          host dispatched retried rate_limited
#>   mygene.info          3       0            0
```

::: {.flow}
::: {}
serve from cache

what is already held
:::

::: {}
send the rest

grouped by host, throttled
:::

::: {}
retry only the retryable

429, timeout, 5xx; honour Retry-After
:::

::: {}
`transport_stats()`

what actually went out
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Results come back in the order you asked. Zip them onto your input by position.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: A gene list is one batch, not N calls, and you can see exactly
what went over the wire.

SCRIPT: Most clients ask many questions of one source. The many variants
take a list, serve what the cache holds, send only the rest, grouped by host
and throttled, and retry only the entries that came back retryable, waiting
what Retry-After asked for. transport_stats tells you what was actually
dispatched, which is the number you want in a log after a big run.

NUMBERS: 3 queries, 1 host.

HONESTY: Batched retry, Retry-After and transport_stats are 0.1.3. On CRAN
0.1.2, max_tries on the batched functions does nothing.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 6:30.

IF ASKED: "Different hosts at once?" That is process level concurrency,
which belongs in the app. httr2 throttles across the whole list, so a mixed
list would make one host wait on another.
:::

## Testing: mocks, and one real server

::: {.walls .g2}
::: {.w3}
`httr2::with_mocked_responses()`

Every status but one. One response object per test. Runs anywhere.

statuses, branching, cache rules
:::

::: {.w1}
`webfakes`

Retry needs a real socket, because mocks sit below the retry loop.

retry, timeout, Retry-After, breaker
:::
:::

```r
httr2::with_mocked_responses(
  list(httr2::response(status_code = 503)),
  expect_identical(mygene_query("BRCA1")$status, "error")
)
```

::: {.payoff}
Worth asserting: a failure is never cached, a 5xx never trips the breaker, a token never prints.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: The whole suite runs offline, and you know which tool to reach for.

SCRIPT: Two tools. For everything except retry, a mocked response is
enough: one status code, one assertion. Retry is the exception because
mocking replaces the transport below the retry loop, so a mocked 503 arrives
once no matter what max_tries says. For that, webfakes runs a real local
server in a second process. Still offline, still deterministic. The three
things worth asserting in your own suite are on the payoff line, because
they are the three that quietly regress.

NUMBERS: 2 tools.

HONESTY: biohttp's own suite never touches a real host.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 7:10.

IF ASKED: "Does webfakes need a network?" No. It binds localhost.
:::

## Start here

::: {.columns .smallish}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[CRAN 0.1.2]{.chip .public}

```r
install.packages("biohttp")
```

[r-universe 0.1.3]{.chip .internal}

```r
install.packages("biohttp",
  repos = "https://samuelbharti.r-universe.dev")
```

0.1.3 adds `retry_after`, batched retry, `ratelimit_*()`, `transport_stats()`.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Write a client in six lines**

```r
mygene_query <- function(symbol) {
  res <- get_json("https://mygene.info/v3",
    path = "query", query = list(q = symbol),
    source = "MyGene")
  if (!res$ok) return(res)
  status_ok(pluck_at(res$data, "hits"), "MyGene")
}
```

No Shiny dependency, on purpose. The app is the caller.
:::
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: Say the two version numbers out loud, once, and hand them a
six line client.

SCRIPT: CRAN has 0.1.2. Everything I showed with retry_after and
transport_stats is 0.1.3, on r-universe, heading to CRAN. A client on top
of it is six lines with no error handling, because there is nothing to
handle.

NUMBERS: 0.1.2 on CRAN, 0.1.3 on r-universe, 14 recursive dependencies.

HONESTY: Do not say when 0.1.3 lands on CRAN.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: done by 7:45.
